endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Data Flow Control: Subcontractors or third parties (including AI subprocessors) must be bound by equivalent DUA terms.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether requiring vendors to disclose subprocessors, give advance notice of changes, and flow down equivalent BAA and DUA terms reduces unprotected downstream access to patient data. The recommendation rests on one framework endorsement from CHAI, which states that subcontractors and AI subprocessors must be bound by equivalent DUA terms.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard in the material supplied. Under GRADE conventions, no certainty rating can be assigned to an effect that has not been measured. The only support is a single framework statement, which reflects expert judgment and does not provide empirical evidence of benefit or burden.

The CHAI governance playbook classifies equivalent DUA terms for subcontractors and AI subprocessors as a must. The endorsement addresses flow-down of obligations. It does not speak directly to disclosure lists or advance notice of changes, so those two elements of the recommendation lack even framework-level support in the sources provided.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether subprocessor disclosure, change notification, and contractual flow-down reduce unauthorized or unprotected downstream data access, and no study supplied documents how often such access occurs with AI vendors. Useful work would include audits of AI vendor contracts for flow-down clauses, counts of undisclosed subprocessors found during review, and comparisons of data incidents between organizations that do and do not enforce these terms.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether contractual protections work equally well for patients served by under-resourced organizations, which may have less capacity to review vendor contracts.
